awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Sublinear Graph Algorithms: New Insights for Foundational Problems
awd_abstract_narration:
Graphs are one of the most natural ways to represent relationships between data and are used to model a wide variety of settings: social networks, the communication infrastructure, the interconnections of financial markets, metabolic processes, and the wiring of the human brain, to name a few. Processing such graphs has long been a cornerstone of computer science research, but the rise of big data poses unique computational challenges, as the scale of the graphs in these applications has far outpaced available computing power. The goal of this project is to develop a new toolkit for processing massive graphs. This project studies a novel set of research questions in the analysis of big data, and the new tools developed can be applied to foundational optimization problems such as shortest paths and matching that are central to applications in computer science, social networks, biology, and computational economics. The focus on foundational problems allows the project to bring together undergraduate and graduate students from a wide range of backgrounds. In additional to PhD mentoring and high-school outreach, the education plan includes research opportunities for undergraduates and the development of a new course in sublinear graph algorithms at Rutgers University.

This project centers on three major challenges to processing massive graphs. The first is that such graphs are too large to fit in the memory of a computer, so the data must be compressed on the fly. The second is that it would take too long for a single computer to process the graph, so the computation is distributed over many machines. The third that is that in many applications the underlying graph is changing over time and it is necessary to respond to these changes locally. The project develops novel tools for tackling each individual challenge. At the same time, the project introduces general frameworks that connect the studies of these different challenges and lead to tools that can overcome a broad set of obstacles simultaneously. More specifically, what unifies the above challenges is the need to extrapolate global information about the entire graph from local information computed in small regions. For example, can one detect overloaded vertices from a small random sample of the graph? How can shortest paths in different regions be patched together to form a path from one end of the graph to another? How can a graph be compressed to only retain the most relevant edges? By answering these and related questions, the research will help extend the motivating applications to significantly larger scales and will lead to new mathematical insights into the structure of graphs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The goal of this project was to develop faster algorithms for computing information about large graphs. Graphs are used to model a wide variety of settings, from communication infrastructure to the functioning of the human brain. As these graphs grow in scale, we require more efficient algorithms for processing them. Below are several such algorithms developed over the course of this project. 

A central result of the project concerns the well-known problem of computing a shortest path between two points. Fast algorithms for this problem have been known since the 1950s for the special case when edge-weights are positive. This case captures many natural scenarios; for example, travel times in road networks are always positive. But many other scenarios are modeled with negative edge weights, such as when the weight corresponds to profits and costs. All previously known algorithms required substantially more time, because they repeatedly revisited large portions of the graph. This project showed that such repeated work can in fact be avoided: it produced a near-linear-time algorithm even in the presence of negative weights, thus resolving a gap that had stood since 1956. We were also able to extend the key ideas behind this algorithm to other variants of shortest-path computation, such as when edges have two different costs that need to be optimized (e.g. time and price).

A second line of work concerns dynamic graph algorithms, which maintain information in a graph that changes over time. Consider, for example, the basic problem of detecting whether there is some path between two vertices. Classic algorithms can solve this problem quickly in a fixed graph, but must recompute the information from scratch if the graph changes. Such recomputation is wasteful and prohibitively time-consuming in many real-world graphs (e.g. road networks, communication networks), so there is a need for dynamic algorithms that can adapt to such changes quickly. This project developed several efficient dynamic algorithms for a variety of problems related to shortest paths and to matching (discussed next).

A third central focus of this project was matching and assignment problems. These problems correspond to the setting where there are two kinds of objects that need to be paired up; for example, tasks assigned to machines, or users to advertisements, or resources to projects. They capture a wide variety of applications from scheduling to object recognition. This project developed several efficient algorithms for these problems, including:

  • More efficient parallel and distributed algorithms that are able to solve the problem much more quickly when computation can be spread across multiple processors 
  • dynamic algorithms that are able to efficiently maintain a good assignment in a graph that is changing over time 
  • a versatile tool for generalizing the scope of matching algorithms.  Many of the most efficient matching algorithms worked only in the special case in which all objects are equivalent; in reality, however, some objects inevitably have higher priority than others. This project gave a general transformation that takes any efficient algorithm for the equivalent-objects case and adapts it to handle differing priorities.

Taken together, these results show that several fundamental graph problems can be solved both faster and in more realistic models than was previously known. The project also introduced techniques that are likely to be useful in the design of future algorithms for large networks and for networks that evolve over time.
